          WESTERN FARMERS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE’S AMICUS CURIAE BRIEF AND
             PUBLIC COMMENT RESPONSIVE TO GOOGLE AND OTHER BRIEFING

                 COMES NOW, Western Farmers Electric Cooperative (WFEC), by and through the

         undersigned attorney, and offers the following:

                         OVERVIEW OF RESPONSES TO ISSUES (a) THROUGH (e)
                                  IDENTIFIED IN ORDER 761449

         1. A business or entity can produce and sell more than one product or service.
         2. When an entity providing otherwise wholesale electricity begins to furnish electricity to any
         end-user who ultimately consumes that energy, those transactions are retail sales of electricity and
         the selling entity is, to the extent of those retail sales, a retail electric supplier under the Retail
         Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act (“RESCTA”) and also a public utility under Oklahoma
         state law.
         3. Such retail sales transactions are not wholesale transactions and are not regulated by Federal
         Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), but are regulated by the Oklahoma Corporation
         Commission (“Commission”) unless an Oklahoma statutory exception or exemption applies to
         state regulation.
         4. Self-supply of electricity is the act of a person or entity generating or creating their own
         electricity and using all of it.
         5. Because a transaction to receive electricity from a second entity – any entity other than itself –
         is described in the BYONG transaction to furnish the electricity to Google, this arrangement is not
         self-supply.



                                                           1
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 27




         6. Because the BYONG transaction is in reality a sale to the ultimate consumer, it is not a wholesale
         transaction.
         7. Because this is electric service furnished to a consumer for ultimate consumption, this is “retail
         electric service” under RESCTA.
         8. Any entity engaged in furnishing retail electric service in Oklahoma is a “retail electric supplier”
         under RESCTA.
         9. To the extent the entity is furnishing retail electricity in Oklahoma, the seller in the BYONG
         model is by the terms of Section 151 of Title 17 of the Oklahoma Statutes a public utility, and is
         to be regulated by the Commission.
         10. Any such entity, if lawfully regulated, may provide retail electric service within a municipality
         only if it has a municipal franchise or it does not utilize public streets and ways.
         11. The Southwest Power Pool (SPP) Integrated Marketplace operates in that manner where load
         forecasts drive transmission planning, accredited capacity requirements, and resource adequacy
         responsibilities.
         12. Consequently, a large load cannot simply elect to receive energy from a third party while
         avoiding the transmission planning, upgrade, and reliability consequences associated with serving
         that load which arise from SPP related requirements.
         13. The Commission possesses constitutional and statutory authority to regulate public utilities
         operating within Oklahoma. Okla. Const. art. IX, §§ 18-20; 17 O.S. § 152.
         14. To the extent an entity furnishes retail electric service to Oklahoma consumers and does not
         qualify for a statutory exemption, the Commission has authority to determine the nature of that
         service and the applicability of Oklahoma utility laws irrespective of how wholesale transactions
         are scheduled or settled within SPP markets.
         15. Google is attempting to exhaust the available transmission facilities and avoid paying its fair
         share – the actual cost of service – for new transmission.


         Why Western Farmers Electric Cooperative (WFEC) submits these Comments

                 WFEC provides these comments as a brief pursuant to its interest and participation in

         Oklahoma’s electric industry. While not a party to this case, WFEC operates as a generating and

         transmission (“G&T”) rural electric cooperative serving seventeen distribution cooperative

                                                           2
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 27




         members in Oklahoma, and is a member of SPP with several roles, including that of Load

         Responsible Entity (“LRE”).

                  WFEC expects Data Centers to flourish in Oklahoma and is currently taking steps to allow

         WFEC’s distribution cooperative members the ability to serve data centers. As a G&T, WFEC

         provides wholesale power and energy to its distribution cooperative members through transmission

         facilities. WFEC does not directly serve retail loads, no matter the size. However, the necessary

         transmission and generation planning, tariffs and rates require WFEC to participate in the process

         of serving all new large loads of its members, including data centers. This is more fully explained

         below.

                  Google's position is that SPP provides the legal and operational framework that allows a

         large-load customer to procure generation through federally regulated wholesale markets while the

         incumbent utility continues to provide retail service. Google’s Brief repeatedly relies on SPP's

         Integrated Marketplace, resource adequacy rules, planning reserve margin requirements, load-

         responsibility framework, and FERC-jurisdictional tariff structure to support that argument.

                  Google's proposal is premised on separating the benefits associated with generation

         resource procurement from the obligations associated with serving load. Under SPP's tariff,

         resource adequacy obligations attach to the LRE, not the customer. The entity responsible for

         serving load must maintain sufficient accredited capacity, satisfy Planning Reserve Margin

         requirements, and cure any deficiencies identified under Attachment AA. Google's proposal seeks

         to independently procure resources for the customer’s benefit while leaving those compliance and

         reliability obligations with the incumbent utility. Because SPP's resource adequacy framework

         does not permit the separation of resource benefits from resource responsibility, Google's proposal

         is inconsistent with the operational and regulatory structure governing service within SPP.


                                                         3
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 27




                 From WFEC’s Perspective, Google is attempting to utilize existing transmission capability

         while avoiding responsibility for transmission upgrades and other transmission expansion costs

         that would otherwise be evaluated and allocated pursuant to the Southwest Power Pool Open

         Access Transmission Tariff ("SPP OATT"). This tariff includes the Integrated Transmission

         Planning ("ITP") process, Attachment O transmission planning requirements, and applicable cost-

         allocation methodologies. Any attempt to serve load outside those tariff possesses risks shifting

         costs to other transmission customers and LREs.

                 In essence, whatever portion of their load that cannot be connected without upgrades,

         Google wants to be served under a BYONG model and avoid upgrade costs that would ultimately

         be put on the next load interconnection customer (potentially not a large load). Google wants to

         take advantage of existing capacity and the infrastructure, which has been paid by other customers.

                 The understanding and determinations of the Commission regarding very large loads and

         the generation and delivery of electric power and energy serving such loads can impact WFEC as

         a market participant and LRE in SPP. Third parties’ sales of electricity to Google or other large

         loads must be recognized as retail sales by third parties and not as a form of self-supply allowed

         under Oklahoma laws. Such a mischaracterization, as proposed in the Google Brief and supported

         in large part by the Joint Brief1 of several parties, would directly affect WFEC and its member

         distribution cooperatives.

                 Various options for serving Google in this case have been presented through testimony,

         arguments and briefing of the several Parties. Some of the options provide certain procedures for




         1
          American Assoc. of Retired Persons, Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers, Oklahoma Sustainability Network,
         the Petroleum Alliance of Okla, and the Public Utilities Division.

                                                              4
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 27




         properly serving this new load. However, the BYONG option requested by Google would raise

         costs for other Oklahoman electric consumers, violate state laws and subvert federal regulations.

         A. Comments on Issues (a) through (e) as identified in the Commission’s Order 761449

         i) BYONG is Not Self-Supply of Electricity

                  Google fails in its Brief in Chief (“Google Brief”) to specify or describe the ‘federal

         wholesale arrangements’ it plans to undertake to receive electric power, energy, capacity or other

         related attributes (herein collectively referred to as electricity). However, to the extent Google

         receives electricity from another person or entity, this is not self-supply.2

                  A literal, historic and legal understanding of self-supply of electricity is simply where a

         person or other entity generates the electricity which that same person or entity uses. The BYONG

         arrangement as proposed relies on a separate party to provide the electric energy and capacity

         requirements. Regardless of the delivery method, contract designation, label, or whether this

         purported wholesale arrangement is regulated or not, this is simply not self-supply.

                  The Google Brief and the Joint Brief consistently conflate “self-supply and BYONG

         arrangement” by using them together to suggest they are one in the same. This combination of

         these two disjoint terms is ubiquitous in both briefs. Because the BYONG arrangement requires

         supply of electricity from another entity, it is not self-supply. The Briefs’ attempts to characterize

         Google’s proposed BYONG as a type of self-supply are simply wrong.

                  Both Briefs, using identical text, begin their arguments by using the two terms as

         interchangeable at Sections II A. of the respective briefs “A. The structure of a self-supply or


         2
          Additionally, any sales of electricity to an end-user inherently create retail sales by a third party. This is noted here
         and will be discussed below, but is not relevant to whether or not BYONG is self-supply.

                                                                      5
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 27




         BYONG arrangement.” The briefs proceed from this sub-heading to consider a BYONG

         arrangement as self-supply. No attempt in either brief is made to explain how BYONG, in

         arranging electricity from another party is self-supply. The fact that Google plans to “arrange” the

         supply of electricity from a wholesale market3 is no more self-supply than Google arranging the

         supply of electricity from OG&E in the retail context.

                  The effectiveness of this conflation is suggested by the briefing of the Attorney General’s

         Office at page 2, where the BYONG arrangement along with other customer proposals seem to be

         referenced as a “self-supply proposal”. Briefing in the PSO matter PUD 2025-75 also appears not

         to have challenged the designation of a self-supply option using a separate party to supply the

         electricity. Failure in these filings to call out an incorrect label or designation does not alter the

         truth or waive an objection to treating the proposed BYONG arrangement as self-supply.

                  The Joint Brief provides more detail around BYONG than the Google Brief. At page 23,

         while attempting to differentiate the BYONG arrangement from retail wheeling, those collective

         parties stated,

                           “A self-supply or BYONG option involves no retail sale by a third party and no
                  transportation service rendered by the incumbent on any third party’s behalf to a retail
                  customer. A properly designed option requires that all self-supply be coordinated with the
                  incumbent and that all retail electric service be supplied through the incumbent. The third-
                  party seller delivers into the SPP market at its settlement location; the incumbent, as the
                  load-responsible entity, serves its retail customer’s entire load from the market and its own
                  resources and bills the customer under its own tariff.

                           The contention that the incumbent is merely wheeling because it is “not generating”
                  the energy its customer consumes substitutes a different test for the statutory one. A retail

         3
          Arranging the purchase of electricity for its own ultimate use from a wholesale market does not alter that the laws
         and regulations treat such sales as retail sales; as is discussed below.

                                                                   6
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 27




                 electric supplier does not cease to be the retail electric supplier because a portion of the
                 energy its customer consumes was procured under a contract the supplier did not sign.”
                 [Underlining not in Joint Brief.]

         Although a retail sale is not conceded in this Joint Brief, this description reaches the only possible

         conclusion: that an arrangement for delivery of electric power to Google is a transfer of ownership

         inherently involving a sales contract or purchase agreement from a second party. The inclusion of

         a second party necessarily removes the transaction from the realm of self-supply of electricity.

                 Actual self-supply is simply a person or entity creating the energy and using it by

         themselves, without second party involvement. Self-supply requires ownership, or an ownership

         interest in the equipment or physical mechanism which creates the electricity. (See Attorney

         General Opinion 2018-5.) That opinion discussed distributed generation as a form of partial self-

         supply. In that context, the opinion addressed the issue of ‘what is self-supply and what is a retail

         sale of electricity’. The opinion indicated that the specific facts of a situation would control

         whether the necessary element of ownership of the generation devices was present. This question

         has not been specifically addressed in Oklahoma courts. However, in the Attorney General Opinion

         determined that some form of ownership of the generation assets was necessary. BYONG

         arrangements fail to provide such an element of ownership to suggest that self-supply will occur.

                 Actual self-supply is allowed under Oklahoma law and does not hamper or even affect4 a

         utility’s ability to serve other customers. Actual self-supply, whether complete or partial, has never

         been unlawful in Oklahoma. In recognition of this, the Joint Brief at p. 29 discusses an incumbent’s

         obligation to serve in the context of service terms existing for decades for “backup, standby, or




         4
          Except for market forces, such as those which impact the available of equipment and labor owned and held by the
         self-supplying entity.

                                                                 7
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 27




         replacement power” in situations where the customer is self-supplying its own electricity. The brief

         follows by stating as a historical fact, “[The Incumbent] does not hold an entitlement to sell a

         particular quantity of energy to a particular customer, any more than it holds an entitlement to

         prevent a customer from installing efficient equipment, curtailing load, or generating its own

         power.” The Joint Brief’s discussion was offered for other purposes, but illustrates there is no

         disagreement that self-supply is allowed. However, a BYONG arrangement is not self-supply.

         ii) Section 151 of Title 17 Does Not Address Self-Supply

                As just noted, self-supply has always been permitted under Oklahoma law. The 2025

         amendments of SB 480 amending Section 151 of Title 17 of the Oklahoma Statutes by replacing

         subsection B., did not address self-supply of electricity. Rather, the amendment dealt with the

         production of electricity by third parties. The new provisions created a specific exemption from

         Commission regulation by removing certain third party suppliers from the definition of a public

         utility. The change in the statute allowed a third party to serve an affiliate, and certain other

         enumerated entities, from generation facilities which were co-located on the same premises as the

         new large load. The amendment did nothing to address or define self-supply of electricity by a

         party to itself. Likewise, as discussed below, subsection B does not address, or remove from the

         definition of public utility, such third parties as are anticipated by a BYONG arrangement. As

         proposed, BYONG generation will be from parties whose generation is not co-located with the

         new load.

         iii) Retail Sales of Electricity

                In Oklahoma, the criteria controlling whether a sale of electricity is wholesale or retail is

         whether the sale is for resale or is a sale to the end-consumer for ultimate consumption. Section


                                                          8
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 27




         158.22 (1) of RESCTA states, “The term "retail electric service" means electric service furnished

         to a consumer for ultimate consumption, but does not include wholesale electric energy furnished

         by an electric supplier to another electric supplier for resale.”

                 Without specificity, the Google Brief appears to plan for electricity purchases from electric

         entities outside Oklahoma. Under the characterization provided, these entities will sell into SPP

         on a wholesale basis. To the extent these third parties sell wholesale into SPP, their sales will not

         be regulated by the OCC, regardless of the location of the physical delivery point to SPP, or the

         location of the generation facility. Those transactions will be exempt from state regulation by the

         Federal Power Act (FPA). 16 U.S.C. § 824.

                 However, to the extent that even traditional wholesale sellers arrange to deliver electricity

         to an end-using consumer, this is a retail sale. As does Oklahoma law, the FPA expressly limits

         wholesale sales jurisdiction to sales "for resale." 16 U.S.C. § 824(d). A transaction in which the

         economic benefit and ultimate use of electric energy is conveyed to an end-use consumer does not

         become a wholesale transaction merely because the energy is scheduled or settled through a

         federally regulated wholesale market. To the extent an entity makes a sale directly to person for

         the electricity’s ultimate use, that entity acts as a retail seller of electricity, and the transaction is a

         retail sale. Additionally, such a supplier is not for that transaction exempt from regulation in

         Oklahoma under 17 O.S. 2025 § 151.

         iv) FERC Jurisdiction is Expressly Limited to Wholesale Sales, the Mischaracterized

         Wholesale Market Transaction of BYONG is Not an Authorized Retail Sales in Oklahoma

                 Google’s Brief and the Joint Brief rely heavily on FERC jurisdiction of wholesale

         transactions. Without question, FERC has exclusive jurisdiction over interstate wholesale sales of


                                                              9
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 27




         electric power and energy. But this is not the issue presented. The issue is whether FERC regulates

         retail sales to end-users in Oklahoma. It does not. Construing the limits of FERC’s jurisdiction

         over sales of electricity supplanting state regulation, the United States Supreme Court stated, “The

         Federal Power Act [] places beyond FERC's power, leaving to the States alone, the regulation of

         “any other sale”—i.e., any retail sale—of electricity. § 824(b).” FERC v. Elec. Power Supply

         Ass'n, 577 U.S. 260, 136 S. Ct. 760, 762, 193 L. Ed. 2d 661 (2016), as revised (Jan. 28, 2016).

         Any retail sale of electricity must conform to Oklahoma law, including RESCTA.

                Numerous federal decisions recognize the complementary jurisdiction of states over retail

         sales, retail service obligations, distribution facilities, and siting matters. The SPP OATT governs

         transmission service and wholesale market participation, but it does not create authority for a non-

         incumbent supplier to provide retail electric service within Oklahoma absent compliance with

         Oklahoma law.

         v) Retail Electric Suppliers under RESCTA

                Even if such BYONG generation supplying entities were considered exempt from

         classification as public utilities pursuant to 17 O.S. 2025 § 151, which they are not, entities

         providing retail electric service in Oklahoma are “electric retail suppliers” as defined by RESCTA

         at 17 O.S. § 158.22(1). As noted above, the statutory definition of "retail electric service" in 17

         O.S. § 158.22 focuses on furnishing electric service for ultimate consumption, not on the identity

         of the scheduling coordinator, balancing authority participant, market participant, or settlement

         entity. Participation in SPP markets does not alter the retail nature of service furnished to an end-

         use customer.




                                                          10
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 27




                  Retail electric suppliers “shall not furnish, make available, render or extend its retail

         electric service to a consumer for use in electric-consuming facilities located within the certified

         territory of another retail electric supplier …”. See 17 O.S. 2025 §158.25 (A). As conceded in the

         Google Brief and Joint Brief, retail electric suppliers in Oklahoma have exclusive rural service

         areas described as certified territories. In those areas, other retail electric suppliers may not

         encroach to make retail sales, even if the customer seeks alternative service. See IOCHEM

         CORPORATION v. OKLAHOMA CORPORATION COMMISSION, 2021 OK CIV APP 28, 497

         P.3d 696.

                  Google attempts to circumvent these exclusive service areas by claiming it will receive

         electricity from third parties via wholesale arrangements. Such claims are as described above

         illusionary attempts to relabel the actual process Google plans to use to receive electricity. For

         both its purchases of electricity from OG&E and from third parties, these are purely retail sales of

         electric power and energy to Google from retail electric suppliers. As such, no exemption applies

         to RESCTA’s exclusive service areas as previously approved by order of this Commission.5

                  At page 14, the Google Brief states, “It [the Southern Oklahoma Power decision6] also

         does not establish that a wholesale-market participant becomes a retail public utility merely

         because its generation supports an Oklahoma customer's load. The brief misses the mark.

         Support of generation, as phrased by Google, through middle sellers or the original generation

         owner can clearly be wholesale in nature. However, in the BYONG arrangement, some party

         other than OG&E is furnishing electricity to Google by way of a contract or other agreement.




         5
           Exclusive service areas or certified territories result from orders of this Commission authorized by 17 O.S. §§
         158.24 and 158.26.
         6
           Southern Oklahoma Power Co. v. Corporation Commission, 1923 OK 939, 96 Okla. 53, 220 P. 370.

                                                                   11
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 27




         This ultimate sale to Google is a retail transaction. Such a transaction is not merely generation

         which supports Google’s load.

                An otherwise actual wholesale market participant, when selling retail, is also a retail

         electric supplier under RESCTA and a public utility under 17 O.S. 2025 § 151, if the generation

         and consumption are not co-located. Here, Google attempts to skip the retail sale and mislabel

         the transaction as wholesale. The Joint Brief does not make such an argument or otherwise

         support Google’s Brief in this regard.

                An SPP market participant, acting in such a capacity, only trades on a wholesale basis

         when buying or selling from SPP. Bilateral sales through SPP are usually wholesale sales. In

         contrast, furnishing electric service to a consumer for the ultimate consumption is the definition

         of “retail electric service” in Oklahoma 17 O.S. § 158.22(4). Any person or entity which

         provided such retail electric service becomes, at least for that transaction, a “retail electric

         supplier.” 17 O.S. § 158.22(1). In its brief, Google avoids any description or analysis of this

         retail transaction, which is a separate retail transaction necessary to deliver electric power and

         energy to a retail end-using consumer.

         vi) The 1MW Exception has No Application with BYONG Arrangements

                Found at subparagraph E of § 158.25 of RESCTA are two exceptions to the exclusive

         service area mandate. Neither applies in the scenario presented by Google’s BYONG.

                Google is not, and will not be, a retail electric supplier and has no retail electric supply

         facilities which it could extend. Therefore, the first exception allowing retail electric suppliers to

         extend service to their own property and facilities does not apply. Likewise, the proposed third

         party supplier is located outside Oklahoma, so as to have no retail supply facilities to which it can

         extend. The 1MW exception to exclusive service does not apply unless a retail electric supplier is

                                                          12
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 16 OF 27




         extending its physical service to serve. See OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC CO. v. STATE ex

         rel. OKLAHOMA CORP. COMMISSION, 2025 OK 15, 565 P.3d 418. Thus, the proposed third

         party cannot meet the 1MW exception to serving in another provider’s exclusive territory.

                    Moreover, assuming a third party as described by BYONG could become a retail electric

         supplier for the purposes of RESCTA, then it cannot serve using an incumbent’s facilities. Instead,

         it must provide service extending its own retail electric facilities and not using or ‘tapping’ another

         provider’s facilities. Id.

                    In their proposed BYONG, Google seeks service from third party generation delivered over

         OG&E lines. The 1MW Exception only allows for a retail electric supplier to extend its own

         service facilities to serve a new load which is to be 1,000 kw (1MW) or larger. The undisclosed

         third party(ies), operating as retail electric supplier(s), could not extend their own non-existent

         facilities to serve Google’s load. Quite to the contrary, Google’s proposal is to require OG&E to

         deliver the third party electricity over OG&E’s retail facilities.

         vii) Retail Service in Municipalities

                    Under Oklahoma law, a public utility furnishing retail electric service within municipal

         boundaries generally must possess lawful authority to occupy municipal rights-of-way through

         franchise authority, or other lawful authorization.7 To the extent a third-party supplier proposes to

         provide retail electric service directly to Google or another end-use customer located within

         municipal boundaries, such supplier must identify the legal authority under which it proposes to

         II. BYONG WILL NOT WORK WITH SPP RULES AND PROCEDURES

                Google's proposal is premised on separating the benefits of generation procurement from

         the obligations associated with serving load. The SPP tariff does not operate in that manner. Under

         Attachment AA, resource adequacy obligations attach to the LRE responsible for serving the load.




                                                         20
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 118 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 11/20/2026 - PAGE 24 OF 27




         The LRE must maintain sufficient accredited capacity to satisfy forecasted demand and applicable

         Planning Reserve Margin requirements.

                Accredited capacity is valuable because it satisfies a reliability obligation. If a resource

         experiences an outage, loses accreditation value, or otherwise becomes unavailable, the obligation

         to cure the resulting deficiency remains with the LRE. SPP does not look to the customer to satisfy

         resource adequacy requirements. SPP looks to the entity responsible for serving the load.

                Google's proposal seeks to claim the benefits of customer-designated generation resources

         while leaving resource adequacy compliance, transmission planning, and reliability obligations

         with the incumbent utility. This creates an impermissible disconnect between authority and

         responsibility. The entity responsible for maintaining compliance must possess sufficient

         contractual rights and control over the resources relied upon to satisfy that obligation. Otherwise,

         the utility remains responsible for deficiencies caused by resources it does not control.

                The same principle applies to transmission planning. SPP plans the transmission system

         based on forecasted load and the resources expected to serve that load. Large load additions drive

         transmission studies, network upgrades, and long-term reliability investments regardless of how a

         customer characterizes its generation arrangements. Those planning and reliability obligations

         remain associated with serving the load and cannot be separated through private contractual

         arrangements.

                If Google contends that customer-designated resources should be credited toward

         satisfaction of the LRE's resource adequacy obligation, those resources must necessarily remain

         subject to enforceable rights sufficient to allow the LRE to ensure ongoing compliance with

         Attachment AA. Resource accreditation and resource responsibility must remain aligned. Google's

         proposal would separate the two and is therefore inconsistent with SPP's resource adequacy

         framework.

                Google's proposal appears premised on the assumption that transmission capacity and

         resource adequacy obligations can be separated from the retail service relationship. SPP's

         Integrated Marketplace and Attachment AA do not operate in that manner. Load forecasts drive

         transmission planning, accredited capacity requirements, and resource adequacy responsibilities.

         Consequently, a large load cannot simply elect to receive energy from a third party while avoiding

         the transmission planning, upgrade, and reliability consequences associated with serving that load.

         Any new or increased transmission requirements must be evaluated through SPP's transmission

         planning and interconnection processes, including Attachment O, Attachment V, and related tariff

         provisions.

                                                      CONCLUSION

                The Commission possesses constitutional and statutory authority to regulate public utilities

         operating within Oklahoma, as well as all retail transactions except to the extent excluded by state

         statute. The proposed BYONG arrangement would result in a retail sale regulated by the

         Commission and, at best, prohibited by RESCTA as a violation of exclusive territory provisions.

                Google's proposal is fundamentally inconsistent with SPP's resource adequacy and

         transmission planning framework because it attempts to separate the benefits of customer-

         designated generation from the obligations that arise from serving load. If customer-designated

         resources are to be credited toward satisfaction of an LRE's obligations, the LRE must have

         enforceable rights and sufficient control over those resources to ensure ongoing compliance. By

         attempting to retain the benefits of designated generation while leaving resource adequacy,

         transmission planning, upgrade costs, and reliability obligations with the incumbent utility,
